drotr: Learning and evaluating threshold-based treatment rules

Allison Codi
allison.codi@emory.edu

Source: vignettes/drotr.Rmd
drotr.Rmd

Abstract

The drotr package implements a cross-validation-based framework for learning, evaluating, and comparing individualized treatment rules. Rules are defined by thresholding estimates of the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) to recommend treatment only when the expected benefit reaches a prespecified clinically meaningful magnitude. The framework allows rules based on different sets of baseline covariates to be compared, facilitating evaluation of the potential value of additional measurements such as diagnostic biomarkers. Nested cross-validation, a doubly robust learner, and Super Learner are used to develop the rules, with augmented inverse probability weighted estimators used to evaluate outcomes and effects under each rule. This vignette introduces the estimands and demonstrates rule learning, evaluation on held-out data, and comparison of treatment rules using data simulated to resemble the AntiBiotics for Children with severe Diarrhea (ABCD) trial.

Introduction

Individualized treatment rules tailor recommendations to patient characteristics. Such rules are useful when the benefit of treatment varies across individuals, but treating everyone with any positive expected benefit may be undesirable. For example, antibiotics can benefit children with bacterial diarrheal illness, yet broad antibiotic use can contribute to antimicrobial resistance. Treatment guidance therefore needs to weigh expected clinical benefit against the consequences of unnecessary treatment.

The drotr package implements the framework described in Machine learning for estimating and comparing clinical rules for treating diarrheal illness with antibiotics (Codi et al.). The approach focuses on two practical questions: who is expected to benefit enough to justify treatment, and which patient characteristics are needed to make useful treatment recommendations? We define rules by thresholding the conditional average treatment effect (CATE), allowing a prespecified minimum magnitude of expected clinical benefit. We then evaluate and compare rules based on different subsets of covariates, including readily available clinical characteristics and potentially more costly diagnostic measurements.

Treatment rules are learned using a doubly robust (DR) learner (Kennedy 2023), with Super Learner used for nuisance and CATE regression estimation (Luedtke and Laan 2016; Montoya et al. 2023). An outer cross-validation procedure separates rule development from effect evaluation. On held-out data, augmented inverse probability of treatment weighted (AIPTW), or one-step, estimators are used to estimate subgroup-specific treatment effects, the proportion recommended treatment, and population-level outcomes under each rule. The resulting inference pertains to the data-adaptive rules learned in the training folds, not to an independently specified fixed rule.

Methods

Notation and treatment rules

Let W∈𝒲W \in \mathcal{W} denote measured baseline covariates and let Z⊆WZ \subseteq W represent the subset of covariates used to make treatment recommendations. Let A∈{0,1}A \in \{0,1\} indicate binary treatment, YY the outcome of interest, and Δ∈{0,1}\Delta \in \{0,1\} an indicator that YY is observed (Δ=1\Delta=1). The observed data consist of independent observations Oi=(Wi,Ai,Δi,ΔiYi)O_i=(W_i,A_i,\Delta_i,\Delta_iY_i), i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. For a∈{0,1}a \in \{0,1\}, let Y(a,1)Y(a,1) denote the outcome that would be observed under treatment aa without outcome missingness. We write Y(a)Y(a) for Y(a,1)Y(a,1) below to match the package’s printed output.

For a particular set of input covariates ZZ, the CATE is

ψ(z)=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣Z=z]. \psi(z)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid Z=z].

A treatment rule d:𝒵→{0,1}d:\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\{0,1\} assigns treatment based on ZZ. Rather than requiring treatment for everyone with any expected benefit, we use a clinically meaningful threshold tt. For a desirable outcome, such as length-for-age z-score, the package defines a rule that recommends treatment for an estimated CATE greater than t>0t>0:

d(Z)=I{ψ(Z)>t}. d(Z)=I\{\psi(Z)>t\}.

For an undesirable outcome, such as the presence of diarrhea, improvement is a reduction in the outcome; the rule recommends treatment when the CATE is less than t<0t<0:

d(Z)=I{ψ(Z)<t}. d(Z)=I\{\psi(Z)<t\}.

The rule is determined by both the selected covariates ZZ and the threshold tt. In estimate_OTR(), positive thresholds specify desirable outcomes and negative thresholds specify undesirable outcomes. For a zero threshold, provide "+0" or "-0" to indicate the desired direction. The package uses strict inequalities when applying the threshold.

Estimands for evaluating a rule

Let Y(d)=d(Z)Y(1)+{1−d(Z)}Y(0)Y(d)=d(Z)Y(1)+\{1-d(Z)\}Y(0) denote the potential outcome if everyone received treatment according to rule dd, and let pd=P{d(Z)=1}p_d=P\{d(Z)=1\} be the proportion recommended treatment. The primary estimands include:

  1. Average treatment effect among those recommended treatment (ATRT): ATRTd=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣d(Z)=1]ATRT_d=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid d(Z)=1].
  2. Average treatment effect among those not recommended treatment (ATNRT): ATNRTd=E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣d(Z)=0]ATNRT_d=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid d(Z)=0].
  3. Proportion recommended treatment: pd=P{d(Z)=1}p_d=P\{d(Z)=1\}.
  4. Average treatment effect under the rule (ATR): ATRd=E[Y(d)−Y(0)]ATR_d=E[Y(d)-Y(0)], comparing use of the rule against a policy of treating nobody.
  5. Difference in subgroup treatment effects: ATRTd−ATNRTdATRT_d-ATNRT_d, evaluating how well the rule distinguishes groups with different expected treatment benefits.

In particular,

ATRd=pdATRTd, ATR_d=p_d\,ATRT_d,

because people not recommended treatment receive the same treatment under rule dd and under the no-treatment policy.

The package also reports outcome levels in addition to treatment effects:

  • E[Y(1)∣d(Z)=1]E[Y(1)\mid d(Z)=1] and E[Y(0)∣d(Z)=1]E[Y(0)\mid d(Z)=1]: expected outcomes under treatment and no treatment among those the rule recommends treating.
  • E[Y(d)]E[Y(d)]: expected population outcome if everyone follows rule dd.
  • E[Y]E[Y]: expected outcome under the observed treatment-assignment process.
  • E[Y(d)−Y]E[Y(d)-Y]: expected difference between outcomes under rule dd and the observed treatment-assignment process.

The last three estimates are included in drotr result objects from version 0.2.0 and later. When an older result object lacks the new quantities, its print method displays --; a computed but undefined estimate remains NA.

Estimation and cross-validation

We use outer KK-fold cross-validation to separate the development of each treatment rule from its evaluation. Each fold has a training sample, used to learn a rule, and an independent held-out validation sample, used to estimate that rule’s performance. The training sample is further divided into VV inner folds to construct a DR learner for the CATE (the package uses three inner folds). This separation reduces overfitting and supports inference on the average performance of the cross-validated, data-adaptive rules.

Within an outer training sample, the DR learner uses three nuisance regressions:

μ(a,w)=E[Y∣A=a,Δ=1,W=w],π(a∣w)=P(A=a∣W=w),γ(1∣a,w)=P(Δ=1∣A=a,W=w). \begin{aligned} \mu(a,w) &= E[Y\mid A=a,\Delta=1,W=w],\\ \pi(a\mid w) &= P(A=a\mid W=w),\\ \gamma(1\mid a,w) &= P(\Delta=1\mid A=a,W=w). \end{aligned}

We fit these regressions using Super Learner. For observation ii in an inner validation fold vv of outer training fold kk, define the pseudo-outcome

D̂k,v(Oi)=(2Ai−1)Δiπ̂k,v(Ai∣Wi)γ̂k,v(1∣Ai,Wi){Yi−μ̂k,v(Ai,Wi)}+μ̂k,v(1,Wi)−μ̂k,v(0,Wi). \widehat D_{k,v}(O_i)= \frac{(2A_i-1)\Delta_i} {\widehat\pi_{k,v}(A_i\mid W_i)\widehat\gamma_{k,v}(1\mid A_i,W_i)} \{Y_i-\widehat\mu_{k,v}(A_i,W_i)\} +\widehat\mu_{k,v}(1,W_i)-\widehat\mu_{k,v}(0,W_i).

Regressing the pseudo-outcome on ZZ in each inner validation fold yields an estimate of the CATE. We average these estimates across the VV inner folds to define the rule learned from outer training fold kk, denoted d̂k\widehat d_k. For a desirable outcome, for example, d̂k(Z)=I{ψ̂k(Z)>t}\widehat d_k(Z)=I\{\widehat\psi_k(Z)>t\}. Under the relevant consistency and rate conditions, the DR construction allows consistent CATE estimation if the outcome regression is consistently estimated or if both the treatment and missingness regressions are consistently estimated (Kennedy 2023).

To evaluate a learned rule on its outer validation sample, we re-estimate the nuisance regressions using the full outer training sample. For a,a′∈{0,1}a,a'\in\{0,1\}, define

θk(a∣a′)=E[E(Y∣A=a,Δ=1,W)∣d̂k(Z)=a′],pk(a′)=P{d̂k(Z)=a′}. \theta_k(a\mid a')= E\!\left[E(Y\mid A=a,\Delta=1,W)\mid\widehat d_k(Z)=a'\right], \qquad p_k(a')=P\{\widehat d_k(Z)=a'\}.

Writing ℐk\mathcal I_k for the held-out observations, nk=|ℐk|n_k=|\mathcal I_k|, and p̂k(a′)\widehat p_k(a') for the observed proportion assigned recommendation a′a' in that sample, the one-step estimator can be expressed as

θ̂k(a∣a′)=1nk∑i∈ℐkI{d̂k(Zi)=a′}p̂k(a′)[I(Ai=a,Δi=1)π̂k(a∣Wi)γ̂k(1∣a,Wi){Yi−μ̂k(a,Wi)}+μ̂k(a,Wi)]. \widehat\theta_k(a\mid a')=\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_k} \frac{I\{\widehat d_k(Z_i)=a'\}}{\widehat p_k(a')} \left[ \frac{I(A_i=a,\Delta_i=1)} {\widehat\pi_k(a\mid W_i)\widehat\gamma_k(1\mid a,W_i)} \{Y_i-\widehat\mu_k(a,W_i)\} +\widehat\mu_k(a,W_i) \right].

The subgroup effects are obtained from θk(1∣1)−θk(0∣1)\theta_k(1\mid1)-\theta_k(0\mid1) and θk(1∣0)−θk(0∣0)\theta_k(1\mid0)-\theta_k(0\mid0); the rule effect additionally uses the proportion treated. Standard errors for these effects and comparisons are based on influence-function calculations and the delta method. The fold-specific estimates are then aggregated over outer validation folds. Because the rules vary across training samples, resulting confidence intervals should be interpreted for the corresponding cross-validated data-adaptive targets, rather than for a prespecified rule.

Usage

First, load the package. The model-fitting examples below are shown but not executed when the vignette is built (eval = FALSE) because nested cross-validation with several Super Learner candidates is computationally intensive. The data setup and learner definitions do run during the build. To reproduce an analysis interactively, execute the relevant model-fitting chunks and their dependent output chunks in order.

First, load the package:

library(drotr)

The example uses abcd_data, a simulated dataset distributed with drotr and designed to resemble data from the AntiBiotics for Children with severe Diarrhea (ABCD) randomized trial. In ABCD, children with acute watery diarrhea were randomized to azithromycin or placebo; the simulated dataset contains n=6,692n=6{,}692 observations and 40 baseline covariates. This illustration uses simulated, not individual-level trial, data.

data(abcd_data)
head(abcd_data[c("pid", "an_grp_01", "lazd90", "agemchild", "shigella_new")])
#>   pid an_grp_01      lazd90 agemchild shigella_new
#> 1   1         0 -0.24423622  5.801993     1.975475
#> 2   2         0 -3.24702621 14.681659     0.000000
#> 3   3         0 -0.05373623  7.558416     0.000000
#> 4   4         0 -2.17004791 13.743810     0.000000
#> 5   5         1  0.17351546  9.848812     0.000000
#> 6   6         1 -2.21432910  9.799398     0.000000

We consider azithromycin (an_grp_01, coded 1 for treatment and 0 for placebo) and length-for-age z-score 90 days after enrollment (lazd90). Approximately 4% of the simulated outcomes are missing. We first construct a host-characteristics rule using a subset of baseline anthropometric, demographic, and socioeconomic covariates (Z) to make recommendations, while allowing the nuisance models to use a broader set (W). With t=0.05t=0.05, treatment is recommended to children whose estimated CATE exceeds a gain of 0.05 length-for-age z-score units.

Higher length-for-age z-scores are desirable, so we use a positive threshold. For an undesirable binary outcome such as diarrhea at day three, a negative threshold would instead identify children whose estimated probability of the outcome decreases sufficiently under treatment. At zero, use the character string "+0" (desirable outcome) or "-0" (undesirable outcome) to specify the direction.

Inputs

Let’s set the parameters described above to be passed into the function:

Y <- "lazd90"

A <- "an_grp_01"

W <- c("rotavirus_new", "rotavirus_bin", "norovirus_new", "norovirus_bin", "adenovirus_new",
      "adenovirus_bin", "sapovirus_new","sapovirus_bin", "astrovirus_new", "astrovirus_bin",
      "st_etec_new", "st_etec_bin", "shigella_new", "shigella_bin", "campylobacter_new",
      "campylobacter_bin", "tepec_new", "tepec_bin", "v_cholerae_new", "v_cholerae_bin",
      "salmonella_new", "salmonella_bin", "cryptosporidium_new", "cryptosporidium_bin",
      "dy1_scrn_vomitall", "dy1_scrn_lstools", "dy1_scrn_sstools", "dy1_scrn_diardays",
      "dy1_scrn_dehydr", "avemuac", "wfazscore", "lfazscore", "wflzscore", "site",
      "dy1_ant_sex", "agemchild", "an_ses_quintile", "an_tothhlt5", "month_en", "rotaseason")

Z_host <- c("avemuac", "wfazscore", "wflzscore", "lfazscore", "dy1_ant_sex", "agemchild", "an_ses_quintile")

t <- 0.05

Next, we need to choose which libraries we are interested in using to fit our nuisance models. The SuperLearner package comes with wrappers for common prediction algorithms (see SuperLearner::listWrappers() for full list of available wrappers). We will choose several for our outcome model that should be able to capture the complex form of the outcome model.

sl.library.outcome <- c("SL.glm", "SL.ranger", "SL.earth")

Because treatment was randomized 1:1 in the motivating ABCD trial, a constant-probability learner such as SL.mean is a natural choice for the treatment propensity model in this example.

sl.library.treatment <- c("SL.mean")

We also model the probability that an outcome is observed, conditional on treatment and measured covariates. The package supports custom Super Learner wrappers; here, we illustrate a candidate regression for missingness based on site and enrollment month, alongside a constant-probability model. These two covariates are motivated by patterns of outcome measurement in the ABCD trial.

SL.missing.1 <- function(Y, X, newX, family, ...){
  sl.missing.1_fit <- glm(Y ~ site + month_en,
                          data = X,
                          family = family)
  # get predictions on newX
  pred <- predict(
    sl.missing.1_fit, newdata = newX, type = 'response'
  )
  # format the output as named list
  fit <- list(fitted_model.missing.1 = sl.missing.1_fit)
  out <- list(fit = fit, pred = pred)
  # give the object a class
  class(out$fit) <- "SL.missing.1"
  # return the output
  return(out)
}
predict.SL.missing.1 <- function(object, newdata, ...){
  pred <- predict(object$fitted_model.missing.1, newdata = newdata, type="response")
  return(pred)
}

Include this wrapper among the candidate missingness models:

sl.library.missingness <- c("SL.mean", "SL.missing.1")

Lastly, specify candidate learners for regressing the DR pseudo-outcome on the treatment-rule covariates ZZ:

sl.library.CATE <- c("SL.glm", "SL.ranger", "SL.earth")

Estimate OTR

Call estimate_OTR() to fit the nuisance and CATE regressions, learn the threshold-based rule, and estimate the corresponding effects. We identify participants with pid, use ten outer cross-validation folds (k_folds = 10), and specify a continuous ("gaussian") outcome. This example can be computationally intensive depending on the learners and available hardware.

set.seed(12345)

results_host <- estimate_OTR(df = abcd_data,
                             Y_name = Y, 
                             A_name = A, 
                             W_list = W, 
                             Z_list = Z_host, 
                             id_name = "pid",
                             sl.library.outcome = sl.library.outcome,
                             sl.library.treatment = sl.library.treatment,
                             sl.library.missingness = sl.library.missingness,
                             sl.library.CATE = sl.library.CATE,
                             threshold = t,
                             k_folds = 10,
                             outcome_type = "gaussian")

As an alternative to the preceding one-call workflow, the analysis can be split into two stages: (1) estimate and retain nuisance regressions and fold assignments, then (2) estimate one or more treatment rules using these fits. You need only run one of the two workflows. Reusing nuisance fits is particularly helpful when comparing rules using different sets of ZZ or thresholds, because the rule evaluations can share fold assignments. We use this staged workflow for the comparison below. First, call learn_nuisance():

set.seed(12345)
nuisance_output <- learn_nuisance(df = abcd_data,
                                  Y_name = Y,
                                  A_name = A, 
                                  W_list = W,
                                  sl.library.outcome = sl.library.outcome,
                                  sl.library.treatment = sl.library.treatment,
                                  sl.library.missingness = sl.library.missingness,
                                  k_folds = 10,
                                  outcome_type = "gaussian")

The returned object includes fold-specific nuisance model fits (nuisance_models), outer fold assignments and DR pseudo-outcomes (k_fold_assign_and_CATE), and inner validation indices (validRows). Supply them to estimate_OTR() to avoid re-fitting the nuisance regressions.

nuisance_models <- nuisance_output$nuisance_models
k_fold_assign_and_CATE <- nuisance_output$k_fold_assign_and_CATE
validRows <- nuisance_output$validRows

results_host <- estimate_OTR(df = abcd_data,
                             Y_name = Y, 
                             A_name = A, 
                             W_list = W, 
                             Z_list = Z_host, 
                             id_name = "pid",
                             sl.library.CATE = sl.library.CATE,
                             nuisance_models = nuisance_models,
                             k_fold_assign_and_CATE = k_fold_assign_and_CATE,
                             validRows = validRows,
                             threshold = t,
                             k_folds = 10,
                             outcome_type = "gaussian")

Once the staged workflow has been run, we can print the estimates using print:

print(results_host)

When run, the printed table reports estimates, standard errors, and 95% confidence intervals. In this example, a positive effect indicates improved length-for-age z-score under azithromycin. The rows have the following interpretations:

  • E[Y(1)∣d(Z)=1]E[Y(1)\mid d(Z)=1] and E[Y(0)∣d(Z)=1]E[Y(0)\mid d(Z)=1]: expected day-90 length-for-age z-scores if children recommended treatment were treated or untreated, respectively.
  • E[d(Z)=1]E[d(Z)=1]: the proportion of children who would be recommended azithromycin under the host-characteristics rule.
  • E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣d(Z)=1]E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid d(Z)=1] (ATRTdATRT_d): treatment benefit in the subgroup selected for treatment. This measures the expected clinical benefit among those recommended treatment.
  • E[Y(1)−Y(0)∣d(Z)=0]E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid d(Z)=0] (ATNRTdATNRT_d): treatment benefit in the subgroup not selected for treatment.
  • E[Y(d)−Y(0)]E[Y(d)-Y(0)] (ATRdATR_d): expected population-level improvement from implementing the rule, compared with treating nobody.
  • ATRTd−ATNRTdATRT_d-ATNRT_d: difference in the average treatment benefit between the two recommendation subgroups. This evaluates whether the rule differentiates children by expected benefit.
  • E[Y(d)]E[Y(d)]: expected population-average day-90 length-for-age z-score if treatment were assigned according to the rule.
  • E[Y]E[Y]: expected outcome under the observed treatment-assignment process.
  • E[Y(d)−Y]E[Y(d)-Y]: expected population-average change from the observed treatment-assignment process to implementing the rule.

One may wish to examine other output in the final full_otr_results object. The full_otr_results object contains the following elements:

  • results (class otr_results)
    This component contains an object of class Results for each requested threshold.

    • threshold = t1 (Results object)
      • aggregated_results: Estimated outcomes, effects, and standard errors aggregated across validation folds
      • k_fold_results: Fold-specific estimates and influence-function components
      • decision_df: Estimated CATEs and treatment recommendations in the held-out observations
      • k_non_na: Folds with estimable subgroup effects (excluding folds recommending treatment to everyone or nobody)
    • threshold = t2 (Results object)
      • Same structure as threshold = t1 if additional threshold(s) specified
    • ...
      • Additional thresholds can be added in the same manner.

  • nuisance_models
    A list of nuisance models used in the analysis.

    • fold 1 (Nuisance object)
      • outcome_model: Model for outcome.
      • treatment_model: Model for the treatment.
      • missingness_model: Model for missing data.
    • fold 2 (Nuisance object)
      • Structure similar to fold 1.
    • ...
      • Up to K nuisance models

  • CATE_models
    A list of CATE models generated during the analysis.

    • fold 1: CATE model results for fold 1.
    • fold 2: CATE model results for fold 2.
    • ...: Up to k CATE models

  • Z_list
    List of covariates used for the CATE model

Model objects may be large, especially when using computationally complex Super Learner libraries. To conserve storage while retaining aggregated estimates and printing functionality, save the smaller otr_results component (results_host$results) rather than the full object if you no longer need the nuisance and CATE fits.

Apply a learned OTR to held-out data

The apply_OTR() function applies an already learned rule to another dataset. Rather than re-learning the CATE, it obtains predictions from previously fitted CATE models and applies the chosen threshold to assign treatment recommendations. It then estimates the proportion recommended treatment, subgroup treatment effects, and population-level outcomes under the resulting rule using the outcome and treatment data from the evaluation sample. This supports evaluating whether a rule developed in one dataset is useful in another population or a previously reserved validation sample.

The evaluation dataset must contain the same CATE predictor variables (Z_list) as the development dataset, together with the outcome (Y_name), treatment (A_name), and the covariates (W_list) needed for outcome, treatment, and missingness estimation. These variables should have compatible coding and measurement definitions across datasets. For this evaluation to estimate causal effects, the dataset needs observed treatment and outcome information (outcomes may be missing for some observations). Predictor-only data can be used to derive recommendations in principle, but do not suffice for the effect-estimation workflow illustrated here.

To illustrate, we partition the simulated abcd_data into nonoverlapping development and evaluation samples. We fit a rule in the development sample using estimate_OTR(), then supply its CATE_models to apply_OTR() to evaluate the rule on the held-out sample. We use the same treatment threshold, t=0.05t=0.05, and the host-characteristic covariates defined above (Z_host). Nuisance models are fitted within the evaluation data using the supplied Super Learner libraries. This example is not executed during vignette builds; to run it, execute its model-fitting and output chunks.

set.seed(12345)

train_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(abcd_data)),
                          size = floor(0.8 * nrow(abcd_data)))
train_data <- abcd_data[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
evaluation_data <- abcd_data[-train_idx, , drop = FALSE]

# Use Z_host as defined in the Inputs section; no earlier fitted model is needed.

# Learn the rule on the train sample only
rule_development <- estimate_OTR(
  df = train_data,
  Y_name = Y,
  A_name = A,
  W_list = W,
  Z_list = Z_host,
  id_name = "pid",
  sl.library.outcome = sl.library.outcome,
  sl.library.treatment = sl.library.treatment,
  sl.library.missingness = sl.library.missingness,
  sl.library.CATE = sl.library.CATE,
  threshold = t,
  k_folds = 5,
  outcome_type = "gaussian"
)

# Apply the learned CATE models to the held-out evaluation data
results_evaluation <- apply_OTR(
  df = evaluation_data,
  CATE_models = rule_development$CATE_models,
  Y_name = Y,
  A_name = A,
  W_list = W,
  Z_list = Z_host,
  id_name = "pid",
  threshold = t,
  sl.library.outcome = sl.library.outcome,
  sl.library.treatment = sl.library.treatment,
  sl.library.missingness = sl.library.missingness,
  k_folds = 5,
  outcome_type = "gaussian"
)

print(results_evaluation)

The returned full_otr_results object has the same general structure as the output of estimate_OTR(). For example, the treatment recommendations and model-specific CATE predictions can be inspected through the decision_df component:

head(results_evaluation$results[[paste("threshold = ", t)]]$decision_df)

For the model-based option, the CATE predictions used to define the rule are obtained by averaging predictions across the supplied trained CATE models before applying the threshold. The reported estimates describe the rule’s performance in the evaluation sample, rather than the cross-validated performance of the rules learned within the training sample. The interpretation of the estimands remains the same as above; for example, E[Y(d)−Y(0)]E[Y(d)-Y(0)] compares the rule with treating nobody, whereas E[Y(d)−Y]E[Y(d)-Y] compares it with the observed treatment-assignment process in the evaluation sample. The same causal identification and estimation assumptions remain relevant.

Alternatively, if treatment decisions are already available as a binary vector (one entry per observation in the evaluation data), apply_OTR() can accept d_pred instead of CATE_models. In that case it evaluates the supplied recommendations without predicting the CATE or applying the threshold again. For evaluating a rule on genuinely external data, nuisance model estimation must also be appropriate for the new population; the example above fits these models on the evaluation dataset rather than reusing models learned on the development data.

Compare OTRs

An important goal of the framework is to compare rules built from different input characteristics. For example, a rule using only readily available host characteristics can be compared with a rule incorporating pathogen diagnostics to investigate the potential value of measuring additional biomarkers. Here we construct a second rule using Shigella quantity and detection variables. Both rules use the same threshold, outcome, nuisance fits, and cross-validation splits, so their comparison uses aligned validation samples. The following code follows the staged learn_nuisance() example above; run those chunks first.

Z_shigella <- c("shigella_new", "shigella_bin")

results_shigella <- estimate_OTR(
  df = abcd_data,
  Y_name = Y,
  A_name = A,
  W_list = W,
  Z_list = Z_shigella,
  id_name = "pid",
  sl.library.CATE = sl.library.CATE,
  nuisance_models = nuisance_models,
  k_fold_assign_and_CATE = k_fold_assign_and_CATE,
  validRows = validRows,
  threshold = t,
  k_folds = 10,
  outcome_type = "gaussian"
)

print(results_shigella)

The compare.otr_results() function compares estimated effects between two rules while accounting for their dependence from being evaluated on the same observations. Here "se" specifies the subgroup effect ATRTdATRT_d for each rule. Other supported comparison targets include the population-level rule effect ("te") and the effect among those not recommended treatment ("se_dZ0").

compare.otr_results(res_rule1 = results_host,
                    res_rule2 = results_shigella,
                    threshold = t, 
                    rule1_comp = "se",
                    rule2_comp = "se")

For this call, the result is ATRTdhost−ATRTdShigellaATRT_{d_{\mathrm{host}}}-ATRT_{d_{\mathrm{Shigella}}}. A negative estimate indicates that the average benefit among those recommended treatment is larger for the Shigella-based rule. Because the rules may select different subgroups, this comparison is not a direct contrast of average outcomes under the two policies, and it should not be described as the difference in mean length-for-age z-scores between the two selected groups. Its primary interpretation is the relative ability of the two input sets to identify children with greater treatment benefit. For population-level benefit, compare ATRdATR_d or the expected outcomes E[Y(d)]E[Y(d)] as appropriate to the scientific question.

Average results across seeds

Rule learning depends on random fold assignments and can vary across repeated runs. To summarize estimates from several runs of the same analysis with different random seeds, average_across_seeds() averages the fold-aggregated estimates and combines the reported standard errors across runs. In this example, each seed refits the entire procedure with a new random split, using the same Shigella predictors. This is a descriptive summary of repeated fits, not a substitute for inference over independent datasets or for the data-adaptive confidence intervals produced by an individual fit.

Z_shigella <- c("shigella_new", "shigella_bin")

results_list <- vector(mode = "list", length = 3)

for(seed in 1:3){
  
  set.seed(seed)
  
  results_shigella_seed <- estimate_OTR(df = abcd_data,
                                   Y_name = Y, 
                                   A_name = A, 
                                   W_list = W, 
                                   Z_list = Z_shigella, 
                                   id_name = "pid",
                                   sl.library.outcome = sl.library.outcome,
                                   sl.library.treatment = sl.library.treatment,
                                   sl.library.missingness = sl.library.missingness,
                                   sl.library.CATE = sl.library.CATE,
                                   threshold = t,
                                   k_folds = 10,
                                   outcome_type = "gaussian")
  
  results_list[[seed]] <- results_shigella_seed
  
}

average_across_seeds(results_list = results_list, threshold = t)
